title: Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter

concept.text: The innovation would be a quantum computation that predicts a measurable property of a molecule, material or quantum field beyond the demonstrated accuracy and resource capabilities of the best available classical calculations, followed by an independent physical experiment that confirms the prediction. Its defining achievement is the conjunction of useful physical prediction, credible computational advantage and experimental confirmation. Demonstrating any one of these separately would not complete the milestone.

Conceptual synthesis: a sign problem arises when a classical simulation must estimate a quantity from contributions that cancel strongly, making accurate sampling prohibitively expensive in the relevant regime. Such problems motivate quantum simulation, but neither a sign problem nor strong entanglement by itself proves that every classical approach will fail. The difficulty must be established for the particular physical model, observable, precision and resources being compared.

Promising targets include real-time dynamics, transport and unresolved ground-state properties of strongly correlated systems. Ground-state predictions remain eligible when they reveal genuinely new physical information beyond competitive classical methods. The milestone concerns predictive capability rather than a fixed processor size or architecture; a suitable special-purpose simulator could be a route, although the supplied evidence does not establish which platform would succeed first.

significance.text: If achieved, this would establish experimentally validated access to a physical quantity that available classical calculations could not predict with controlled uncertainty at comparable resources. It would advance the original scientific motivation for quantum simulation: using a controllable quantum system to understand quantum matter that is difficult to calculate classically. The immediate result would be trustworthy new information about the demonstrated observable and regime.

Repeated successes could expand quantitative prediction across nonequilibrium dynamics, transport and strongly entangled ground states. One successful calculation would validate its particular prediction and protocol; it would not automatically establish reliable performance across those domains. The applications perspective identifies nonequilibrium dynamics as an area where classical methods struggle, while treating the broader application vision as speculative and long term.

A commercial catalyst or a room-temperature superconductor would be a conditional downstream possibility requiring further scientific and engineering advances. Predicting one property does not by itself establish how to synthesize a material, whether it remains stable under useful conditions or whether it can be manufactured economically. Experimental verification is necessary for the proposed predictive milestone, but verification alone does not establish commercial utility.

A machine capable of cryptographically relevant Shor computations would not automatically supply this capability. Quantum simulation additionally requires suitable algorithms, preparation of the relevant state, accurate extraction of observables and validation of the physical model. The molecular simulation work provides a concrete example of why hardware scaling alone is insufficient: its outlook identifies algorithmic approximation errors that also need improvement.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is an end-to-end prediction whose quantum uncertainty is quantified, whose classical competitors cannot match its accuracy or resource use and whose physical interpretation survives an independent experimental test. The supplied evidence motivates this target and documents progress toward its components. It does not establish that the complete milestone remains unmet throughout the field as of November 1, 2026.

Target selection must keep pace with classical progress. Tensor networks, Monte Carlo, neural quantum states and other approaches have different strengths, and failure of one technique does not establish a general classical barrier. Dynamics and observables affected by sign problems are promising candidates, alongside unresolved ground-state questions. The supplied perspective reports that few verifiable quantum simulation problems have convincingly established average-case asymptotic speedups. That assessment is distinct from demonstrating a practical advantage on a particular finite instance.

FeMoco illustrates the need to specify the scientific target precisely. A 2024 classical extrapolation paper reports chemical accuracy for strongly correlated calculations that include FeMoco. The supplied abstract does not provide enough detail about the Hamiltonian, active space or error assessment to determine exactly how that result relates to the broader chemical question. The applications perspective still describes FeMoco's electronic structure as unresolved at the accuracy needed for definitive chemical insight. These statements may concern different scopes; they do not justify dismissing either the classical result or ground-state chemistry as a worthwhile quantum target.

The engineering challenge extends beyond executing a large circuit. A useful prediction must control state-preparation errors, device errors, simulation approximations and measurement uncertainty. It must also establish that the chosen Hamiltonian represents the laboratory system closely enough for agreement or disagreement to be scientifically meaningful. The reviewed molecular work demonstrates preparation, measurement and spectroscopic comparison at small scale, while identifying approximation errors that complicate extension to larger spin systems.

current_state.text: Friesecke, Barcza and Legeza's 2024 Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation paper introduces DMRG-RAS-X, an extrapolation method based on restricted-active-space density matrix renormalization group calculations. Its abstract reports chemical accuracy for strongly correlated examples including FeMoco. This documents a significant classical competitor to quantum chemistry benchmarks. The supplied evidence is an abstract record rather than the full paper, so it does not establish the detailed calculation scope or provide an independent audit of the claimed accuracy. The numerical meaning of chemical accuracy is also not defined in that supplied text.

In October 2025, Google reported many-body measurements using out-of-time-order correlators, or OTOCs, which probe how quantum dynamics spreads information. The associated Nature paper claimed beyond-classical performance for selected benchmarking circuits and demonstrated Hamiltonian learning using classically generated toy-model data. Its discussion presented these results as a path toward practical quantum advantage. They did not establish a new prediction about a laboratory material with both independent experimental confirmation and demonstrated computational advantage.

A separate molecular study described in Google's October 22, 2025 account used quantum simulations of nuclear-spin systems requiring nine and fifteen qubits. It compared quantum results with exact classical simulations and independent spectroscopic measurements. This is substantive physical validation at small scale. The accompanying blog explicitly states that this molecular demonstration was not beyond classical capabilities. The remaining distinction is therefore the combination of physical validation with demonstrated computational advantage, rather than physical validation alone.

The strength of the circuit advantage comparison has qualifications. The Nature supplement describes a gate-removal heuristic whose estimated time to solution roughly matches the quantum processor for an OTOC calculation, while emphasizing that its accuracy has little guarantee. The peer-review record also retains objections to broad exclusions of neural quantum states: strong entanglement is not itself a limiting factor for those methods. Neither qualification supplies a demonstrated accurate classical reproduction of the target circuits, but both limit how broadly the comparison can be generalized.

The supplied review had the complete Nature main article, but only partial supplementary and peer-review material. Supplement extraction skipped some form content and was truncated; figure images were not independently inspected, limiting assessment of detailed classical comparisons. The arXiv applications perspective was also partially retained, with relevant application discussions present but detailed supplementary neural-state analysis outside the excerpt. Its displayed December 2025 version date and August 2026 manuscript date were inconsistent. These limitations leave some comparisons and chronology uncertain without invalidating the documented demonstrations. No later field-wide search record was supplied, so the evidence does not settle the milestone's overall status on November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: publish the Hamiltonian, observable, target precision and comparison protocol before the quantum run. Select a scientifically meaningful physical quantity, with at least one case involving dynamics or another observable affected by a sign problem. A ground-state target can qualify when it meets those requirements and provides new physical information. These are proposed evaluation rules, rather than established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Sign-problem target and comparison protocol published before the quantum run

completion_criteria.text: Proposed computational comparison: quantify the quantum result's uncertainty and demonstrate accuracy or resource performance that the best available classical calculations cannot match at publication. Include competitive exact and approximate methods, their convergence evidence, uncertainty estimates and resource costs. Merely obtaining a value outside classical error bars is insufficient: the discrepancy could reflect incorrect classical uncertainty estimates, quantum error or an inconsistent comparison.
completion_criteria.label: Unmatched quantified quantum accuracy or resources versus best classical calculations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed physical confirmation: a later independent laboratory experiment should agree with the advance prediction within a prespecified combined uncertainty. That uncertainty should include quantum computation error, experimental measurement error and uncertainty in the mapping between the Hamiltonian and the physical system. The protocol should distinguish an advance prediction from parameters adjusted after the experimental outcome becomes known.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratory confirmation of advance prediction within prespecified combined uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: release enough model, algorithm, calibration, measurement and resource information for independent scrutiny, and repeat the result sufficiently to establish stability. Independent replication or cross-checking with another device would strengthen the case. Report the demonstrated system sizes, regimes and precision explicitly. A finite set of successes establishes breadth within those tests, not literal universality or a general asymptotic complexity separation.
completion_criteria.label: Information released for scrutiny with the result repeated and limits stated

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: neither a few hundred logical qubits nor use of a near-term device is a completion requirement. The relevant resources depend on the chosen prediction and comparison. Likewise, chemical accuracy should not serve as a universal threshold for dynamics, transport or other observables; each target needs a scientifically justified precision requirement. The supplied abstract uses the term chemical accuracy but does not establish its numerical definition, so no numerical convention is imposed here.
completion_criteria.label: Scientifically justified precision without fixed qubit, device or chemical accuracy

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, concerns a general computational capability that could support QUA-03. QUA-03 adds a specific scientific result and independent physical validation. QUA-02, Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor's algorithm, establishes a different application capability; success at factoring would not establish simulation accuracy, observable extraction or predictive agreement with experiment.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature, concerns quantum memory. QUA-05, Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons, concerns a route to universal computation. Either could contribute enabling technology, but QUA-03 does not require either mechanism and would not establish either milestone through a successful physical prediction.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-06, Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules, and QUA-08, Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls, address scaling and error-correction architecture. QUA-10, Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator, addresses fabrication and operating conditions. These advances could change the feasibility and cost of a QUA-03 calculation, while remaining distinct from demonstrating its scientific prediction.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07, A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems, is a mathematical complexity milestone. A finite experimentally confirmed simulation advantage would not prove that separation. QUA-09, An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data, shares the need for a credible full-resource comparison, but concerns a different input and application setting. QUA-03 does not require a superpolynomial speedup theorem.

QUA-03 also overlaps with Hamiltonian learning, spectroscopy and classical simulation benchmarking. Hamiltonian learning infers a model from observations; spectroscopy supplies physical measurements; classical benchmarking establishes the strength of competing calculations. Each can support the proposed predictive milestone, but none individually establishes its complete combination of advance prediction, computational advantage and experimental confirmation.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete milestone had been achieved elsewhere by November 1, 2026; no field-wide freshness search record was supplied.

The precise Hamiltonian, active-space scope and uncertainty basis of the FeMoco chemical-accuracy claim remain insufficiently documented to reconcile it definitively with the perspective's broader chemical-insight claim.
The accuracy and competitiveness of the gate-removal heuristic, and the scope of viable neural-quantum-state competitors, remain unresolved for the reported circuit benchmarks.
Truncated supplementary and peer-review records, skipped PDF form content and uninspected figure images prevent a complete assessment of detailed classical comparisons.
The arXiv perspective's displayed December 2025 version date and August 2026 manuscript date remain inconsistent.
No concrete Hamiltonian, observable, target precision or feasible independent experimental protocol has been selected for the proposed completion test.
The supplied texts do not establish which hardware platform would reach the milestone first or what qubit count and total resources it would require.

brief.title: Predicting matter beyond ordinary computers
possible: Researchers could predict how a hard-to-calculate molecule or material behaves before testing it in a laboratory. A quantum computation would reach beyond the accuracy or computing resources of the best conventional calculations, and an independent experiment would confirm its prediction.
why: Scientists would gain trustworthy physical information that conventional calculations could not provide. Repeated successes could extend prediction to how quantum matter changes over time, carries current or settles into its lowest-energy state.

sources.who: Ryan Babbush and colleagues, Google Quantum AI
sources.showed: Their perspective identifies obstacles between quantum algorithms and useful applications, including finding concrete problems that outperform conventional computation and yield testable answers.
sources.cited_for: Useful quantum predictions need both a defensible computational advantage and a way to test their answers.
sources.not_established: The perspective does not demonstrate an independently confirmed physical prediction beyond conventional computation.

sources.quote: We observed the signature of this amplification in OTOC signals.
sources.cited_for: Quantum computers can produce measurable signals on difficult test circuits.
sources.not_established: The circuit tests did not deliver a new material prediction confirmed independently; the separate molecular tests remained within conventional capabilities.

sources.showed: They reversed quantum evolution repeatedly to reveal correlations otherwise hidden in the system. They also demonstrated learning a physical model from computer-generated example data.
sources.quote: In response, we find that OTOCs are more sensitive to these perturbations compared with observables in the absence of time reversal.
sources.cited_for: Time reversal can expose measurable details of quantum dynamics that are difficult to calculate conventionally.
sources.not_established: The work did not combine an advance physical prediction, independent laboratory confirmation and demonstrated computational advantage.

shown: Google Quantum AI and collaborators reported performance beyond conventional computation for selected quantum test circuits. Separately, Google's small molecular simulations agreed with exact conventional calculations and independent laboratory measurements.
These demonstrations establish different pieces of the goal. The molecular results provide physical validation, while the circuit results support a computational advantage for particular tests.
missing: An advance physical prediction that combines a demonstrated computational advantage with independent laboratory confirmation.
A complete uncertainty estimate covering computation, laboratory measurement and how faithfully the model represents the physical system.
A repeatable result with enough disclosed detail to assess its accuracy, computing costs and limits.

milestones.label: A physical target and fair comparison specified in advance
milestones.explanation: The model, measured quantity, precision and comparison would have to be published before the run, including a sign-problem case where cancelling contributions hinder conventional simulation. This defines a meaningful test.

milestones.label: Measured quantum performance that conventional calculations cannot match
milestones.explanation: The quantum result would have to quantify its uncertainty and beat the best available conventional calculations on accuracy or computing resources at publication. This establishes the computational advantage.

milestones.label: An independent experiment confirms the advance prediction
milestones.explanation: A later independent experiment would have to agree within a preset uncertainty covering computation, measurement and the physical model. This tests whether the prediction describes nature.

milestones.label: Repeatable results with disclosed methods and stated limits
milestones.explanation: The work would have to disclose enough model, algorithm, calibration, measurement and resource detail for scrutiny, repeat the result and state its tested limits. This establishes stability and the boundaries of the claim.

milestones.label: Precision justified by the physical question
milestones.explanation: The target would have to justify its required precision without a fixed quantum-bit count, device type or universal chemistry threshold. This ties success to the physical question.

uncertain: Which physical target offers both a defensible computational advantage and a feasible independent laboratory test remains open.
How accurately competing conventional methods can reproduce the reported test circuits remains unresolved.
The hardware platform and total computing resources needed remain unknown.

page.title: Experimentally validated quantum advantage in simulation
page.definition: A controllable quantum system predicts a measurable property of a molecule, material or quantum field. In a classical Monte Carlo calculation of that property, positive and negative contributions nearly cancel, making the average hard to estimate by sampling. The quantum simulation uses fewer computational resources than the best available classical method at the same accuracy. An independent laboratory subsequently measures the same property and confirms the prediction within the stated uncertainty.

goal.need: In a model of interacting electrons on an 8 × 8 lattice, estimating spin correlations took up to 4,000 Monte Carlo runs of 200,000 measurement sweeps each at densities with severe cancellations. Cooling the model raises the sampling cost exponentially, while cheaper approximations can bias the correlations. If the model captures the material and other classical methods also fall short, quantum predictions could help physicists test which interactions cause electrons to pair in high-temperature superconductors.

completion.title: An independent experiment confirms a new quantum prediction with demonstrated computational advantage.
completion.criterion: For one specified molecule, material or quantum field and observable in a regime with a documented Monte Carlo sign problem, a quantum simulation produces a prediction before the confirming measurement. At the same accuracy, the best available classical methods cannot match its resource cost. An independent laboratory subsequently measures that observable and agrees within the combined uncertainty specified before measurement, including computation, measurement and model-to-system errors. Both advantage and confirmation must concern the same prediction.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; an operational definition combining published quantum-advantage and physical-verification goals.
completion.basis: Searched DOE scientific-utility goals, Google's application framework, DARPA QBI criteria and XPRIZE Quantum Applications guidelines; none specifies this combined sign-problem, computational-advantage and subsequent independent-confirmation test. The criterion combines Google's finite-resource definition of advantage with its example of confirming a predicted material property by creating and measuring the material. These sources provide no universal accuracy or confidence threshold.

milestones.title: A quantum simulator reproduces dynamics that can be calculated analytically or numerically.
milestones.criterion: Compare the measured evolution of a controllable quantum system with an analytical or numerical solution of the target model in a regime where that solution can be computed. Assess agreement at the accuracy reported for the comparison.
milestones.set_by: Classical cross-checking convention, documented by Shaffer and colleagues in the introduction to their verification study.
milestones.threshold_quote: validation of simulation results is typically performed by comparison to results calculated analytically or numerically

milestones.title: A molecular parameter inferred from quantum spin echoes agrees with spectroscopy within experimental error.
milestones.criterion: Fit a molecular structural parameter by comparing quantum simulations of nuclear spin echoes with measured nuclear magnetic resonance data. Compare the fitted parameter with an independent spectroscopic determination of the same quantity and obtain agreement within experimental error.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI and collaborators, molecular-geometry learning protocol; this comparison was published for molecular nuclear-spin simulations.
milestones.threshold_quote: continues to agree with the reference data within experimental error.

milestones.title: A quantum echo resolves an observable at SNR above 1 beyond competitive classical simulation.
milestones.criterion: Estimate the echo observable across circuit instances with a signal-to-noise ratio above 1. The protocol defines this ratio as 1/√[2(1−ρ)], where ρ is the Pearson correlation between measured and ideal observable values across the instances. Compare the cost with exact classical simulation and with approximate classical algorithms at the achieved accuracy. Distinguish a ratio obtained by direct comparison from one projected using an error model.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI and collaborators, Nature conclusion, criteria (1) and (2); SNR above 1 is their observable-protocol threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: in our case with an SNR above unity.

milestones.title: A quantum simulation predicts a measurable physical property beyond accuracy-matched classical methods.
milestones.criterion: For a specified molecule, material or quantum field with a documented Monte Carlo sign problem in the calculation at issue, use a quantum simulation to predict a measurable property and give its uncertainty before the confirming measurement. Show that the best available exact and approximate classical methods cannot predict that property at the same accuracy within the quantum calculation's resource cost.
milestones.set_by: Google Quantum AI and collaborators, observable criteria (1)–(3), applied here to a prediction for a physical target with a documented sign problem.
milestones.threshold_quote: The observable should yield practically relevant information about the quantum system.

not_found: No located report established the complete conjunction of a sign-problem target, computational advantage and subsequent independent experimental confirmation.

results.quote:
In this pre-print, which will be submitted for peer review, we measured OTOCs on two organic molecules dissolved in liquid crystal at the
Pines Magnetic Resonance Center
at UC Berkeley. This experiment was then simulated on our Willow chip, resulting in improved models of the molecular structure.

results.finding: For 65-qubit Willow echo circuits, the authors estimated a 13,000-fold classical runtime penalty. The circuit count is unspecified.
results.detail: The blog attributes the benchmark to a Nature paper. The classical runtime is an estimate.
results.quote: Our experiments on Willow took approximately 2 hours, a task estimated to require 13,000 times longer on a classical supercomputer.

results.finding: First-order OTOC in 40-qubit random circuits, with the instance count unspecified for this comparison, agreed with exact simulation at SNR 5.4.
results.detail: The reported SNR uses centered, rescaled values across circuit instances and measures agreement in circuit-to-circuit variation.
results.quote: The SNR achieved by CMC (5.3) is close to the experimental SNR of 5.4.

results.finding: The off-diagonal second-order OTOC in 65-qubit circuits had a projected SNR of 2–3. The instance count is unspecified in the supplied text.
results.detail: The 65-qubit SNR and Frontier runtime are estimates. The main text labels the timed quantity as the diagonal component, while the Fig. 4c caption identifies it as the off-diagonal component.
results.quote: Based on the same error model, the SNR of the 65-qubit dataset is projected to range from 2 to 3.

results.finding: Dual-unitary kicked Ising autocorrelation decay closely matched exact theory through 91 qubits, with 262,144 shots per data point.
results.detail: The Clifford-point data were used to calibrate the noise model. The non-Clifford data provided a separate test, with small residual deviations at larger circuit volumes.
results.quote: We demonstrate that with error mitigation we can accurately recover the exact prediction of this decay constant for all system sizes studied.

results.finding: Kicked Ising local Pauli-X estimates from 262,144 shots per point generally agreed with Heisenberg tensor networks at bond dimension 500.
results.detail: Away from dual unitarity, the measured quantity is a local expectation value. The Heisenberg-picture calculations also showed convergence at smaller bond dimensions.
results.quote: Across the different parameters, the experimental data show strong agreement with the Heisenberg simulations with some deviations arising at larger circuit volumes, but large disagreements with the Schrödinger-picture simulations.

results.finding: Willow’s deeper 23-qubit first-order echo reached a directly benchmarked SNR of 5.26 across 50 circuit instances.
results.detail: The deeper layout had 164 two-qubit gates. Tensor network Monte Carlo achieved higher SNR on its 25-instance subset. The 65-qubit belief-propagation cost is extrapolated from smaller simulations and a scaling argument.

definition = "A controllable quantum system predicts a measurable property of a molecule, material or quantum field. In a classical Monte Carlo calculation of that property, positive and negative contributions nearly cancel, making the average hard to estimate by sampling. The quantum simulation uses fewer computational resources than the best available classical method at the same accuracy. An independent laboratory subsequently measures the same property and confirms the prediction within the stated uncertainty.". Reason: The definition needs to locate the sign problem in a classical representation and make clear that the resource comparison and the independent measurement concern the same observable.

goal.need = "In a model of interacting electrons on an 8 \u00d7 8 lattice, estimating spin correlations took up to 4,000 Monte Carlo runs of 200,000 measurement sweeps each at densities with severe cancellations. Cooling the model raises the sampling cost exponentially, while cheaper approximations can bias the correlations. If the model captures the material and other classical methods also fall short, quantum predictions could help physicists test which interactions cause electrons to pair in high-temperature superconductors.". Reason: The example calculation for the mean sign leaves out the cost of estimating a physical observable and the question that a reliable prediction would help answer.

add statement by US Department of Energy, Quantum Genesis Priority Applications, 2026: "on lattice sizes beyond what is currently possible with classical computers.". Reason: The Department of Energy's application document identifies a specific materials calculation and the classical limit it seeks to exceed.

add statement by National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Advancing Chemistry and Quantum Information Science, 2023: "how quantum-accelerated calculations could solve chemistry problems (that otherwise cannot be solved using classical systems)". Reason: The National Academies identifies the chemistry goal and qualifies what noisy devices can achieve without error correction.

edit m1: title = "A quantum simulator reproduces dynamics that can be calculated analytically or numerically."; criterion = "Compare the measured evolution of a controllable quantum system with an analytical or numerical solution of the target model in a regime where that solution can be computed. Assess agreement at the accuracy reported for the comparison.". Reason: The title excludes numerical cross-checks accepted by the cited convention, and the criterion includes the outcome of an oscillator experiment.

edit m2: title = "A molecular parameter inferred from quantum spin echoes agrees with spectroscopy within experimental error."; criterion = "Fit a molecular structural parameter by comparing quantum simulations of nuclear spin echoes with measured nuclear magnetic resonance data. Compare the fitted parameter with an independent spectroscopic determination of the same quantity and obtain agreement within experimental error.". Reason: The criterion mixes one molecule's measured distance with the test and obscures which data are used for fitting and which provide the independent check.

edit m3: title = "A quantum echo resolves an observable at SNR above 1 beyond competitive classical simulation."; criterion = "Estimate the echo observable across circuit instances with a signal-to-noise ratio above 1. The protocol defines this ratio as 1/\u221a[2(1\u2212\u03c1)], where \u03c1 is the Pearson correlation between measured and ideal observable values across the instances. Compare the cost with exact classical simulation and with approximate classical algorithms at the achieved accuracy. Distinguish a ratio obtained by direct comparison from one projected using an error model."; threshold_quote = "in our case with an SNR above unity."; threshold_ref = 10. Reason: The echo benchmark uses a specific correlation across circuit instances, which the existing criterion leaves undefined while reporting projected runtimes and accuracy.

edit m4: title = "A quantum simulation predicts a measurable physical property beyond accuracy-matched classical methods."; criterion = "For a specified molecule, material or quantum field with a documented Monte Carlo sign problem in the calculation at issue, use a quantum simulation to predict a measurable property and give its uncertainty before the confirming measurement. Show that the best available exact and approximate classical methods cannot predict that property at the same accuracy within the quantum calculation's resource cost."; set_by = "Google Quantum AI and collaborators, observable criteria (1)\u2013(3), applied here to a prediction for a physical target with a documented sign problem."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "The observable should yield practically relevant information about the quantum system."; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10, 3, 1]. Reason: The last milestone applies the echo-specific accuracy cutoff to every physical property and includes results on model circuits in the criterion.
structure = parallel. Reason: Agreement with molecular spectroscopy and an advantage on an echo benchmark test different claims, and neither requires the other to occur first.
